meta.description: Quote Investigator traces the famous book-review insult to Bill Miller in 1929. Dorothy Parker’s name was attached in 1962, without a source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'This is not a novel to be tossed aside lightly. It should be thrown with great force'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Dorothy Parker. Quote Investigator credits Bill Miller, who printed it as a joke blurb in his own 1929 book.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — actually Bill Miller
answer.authorDates: American newspaper columnist and boxing publicist · published To You I Tell It in 1929
answer.sourceLine: The joke first appears in To You I Tell It (1929), a self-published book by the columnist and boxing publicist Bill Miller, among a set of deliberately absurd mock endorsements. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that Miller wrote all of those blurbs himself and coined this one; Dorothy Parker’s name was attached to it decades later, in 1962, with no citation attached.

source.excerpt: FRANK DOLAN, New York— Not a book to be lightly thrown aside. Should be thrown with great force.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ gives the earliest known match as 1929, in the self-published To You I Tell It by the newspaper columnist and boxing publicist Bill Miller (William Eli Miller). The book collected mock endorsements “supposedly written by well-known people”; this one was printed over the name of Frank Dolan.

That the attributions were fake is not an inference. QI quotes a December 1929 review by the sports columnist Frank MacDonell, which reprints several blurbs and states that Miller “wrote the recommendations himself” — see the citation list ↗. QI credits Bill Miller with originating the remark, crediting researcher Bill Mullins with finding the 1929 book.

The path to Parker is documented step by step. In 1958 Sid Ziff quoted the line in the Mirror News of Los Angeles and expressly attributed it to an unnamed critic; Reader’s Digest reprinted it in February 1960 ↗ crediting Ziff, dropping his “one critic said” hedge. In 1962 the publisher Bennett Cerf ↗ printed a reworded version in his syndicated column over Parker’s name, with no citation. QI’s verdict: “there is no substantive evidence that she ever employed it.”

The wording most people know today comes from The Algonquin Wits ↗, Robert E. Drennan’s 1968 collection, which listed it in the Dorothy Parker chapter. Wikiquote also files the line under Misattributed ↗, noting that Drennan’s apparent source was a Parker review that does not contain the quote.
source.excerptNote: The blurb as printed in Miller’s 1929 book, transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. The credit to Frank Dolan is part of the joke: a December 1929 review by the sports columnist Frank MacDonell stated plainly that Miller “wrote the recommendations himself”.

source.rightsNote: The 1929 wording shown above is in the public domain in the United States: it was published in Bill Miller’s To You I Tell It in 1929, well before 1931. Note that the familiar modern phrasing — “This is not a novel to be tossed aside lightly” — is not the 1929 text; it comes from Bennett Cerf’s 1962 column and Robert E. Drennan’s The Algonquin Wits (1968), both of which are modern and in copyright. Reuse the 1929 sentence freely; treat the later rewording as you would any 1960s publication. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Bill Miller
author.heading: About Bill Miller
author.metaLine: American newspaper columnist and boxing publicist · active 1920s
author.bio: Bill Miller (William Eli Miller) was an American newspaper columnist and boxing publicist. In 1929 he self-published To You I Tell It and filled its endorsement pages with mock blurbs attributed to well-known writers and sportswriters — all of them, a contemporary reviewer confirmed, written by Miller. One of those invented endorsements outlived the book, the joke and its author, and is now quoted worldwide under somebody else’s name. Little else about him is recorded in the sources we could reach, so we claim no dates for him.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a joke that has been misattributed twice over — once on purpose, as part of the gag, and once by accident, thirty years later.

items.why: Quote Investigator states ↗ that “there is no substantive evidence that she ever employed it”. Her name was attached by Bennett Cerf in a 1962 column with no citation, and multiple researchers have failed to find the joke anywhere in her writings.
Miller printed the blurb over Dolan’s name as part of the book’s running gag. A December 1929 review by Frank MacDonell, quoted by QI ↗, says Miller wrote all the recommendations himself.
In 1975 the columnist Earl Wilson reported the line as Groucho Marx’s remark about a new novel — one more reassignment in QI’s chronology ↗, and no better sourced than Parker’s.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Bill Miller’s, written in 1929 as a fake endorsement of his own book — see Quote Investigator’s full chronology ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke was born already misattributed. Miller’s book printed a page of glowing endorsements from famous names, every one of them invented, and this was the funniest of them — a blurb that insults the book it is advertising. Detached from that page, it stops being a self-deprecating gag and becomes a critic’s kill shot, which is the form in which it travelled.

The rest is a chain of small, ordinary losses. Ziff quoted it in 1958 and said a critic said it; Reader’s Digest reprinted Ziff and dropped the hedge; Cerf supplied a famous name in 1962; Drennan’s 1968 anthology fixed the wording. No one fabricated anything outright. Each step just discarded a qualifier.
detailsBody: The book being insulted is often named as Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged, or as Mussolini’s The Cardinal’s Mistress, which Parker did review in 1928. Quote Investigator addresses both: the Mussolini review does not contain the jest, and QI has located no support at all for the Atlas Shrugged claim. The original target was Miller’s own book.

QI credits the researcher Bill Mullins with locating the 1929 book and the December 1929 review that together settled the question, and Sam Clements and Bonnie Taylor-Blake for the 1960 and 1962 citations.
context.pull: The joke was born already misattributed — and that was the point.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator gives the earliest known match as 1929 in Bill Miller's self-published "To You I Tell It", printed over the name Frank Dolan as "Not a book to be lightly thrown aside. Should be thrown with great force."

Quote Investigator quotes a December 1929 review by Frank MacDonell stating Miller wrote the recommendations himself, and concludes there is no substantive evidence Dorothy Parker ever employed the quip; Bennett Cerf reassigned it to her in 1962 without a citation.

Wikiquote files "This is not a novel to be tossed aside lightly. It should be thrown with great force." under Misattributed on its Dorothy Parker page, noting Drennan's apparent source is a Parker review that does not contain the quote.
Wikipedia gives Bennett Alfred Cerf, May 25 1898 – August 27 1971, an American writer, publisher and co-founder of Random House.
The Internet Archive holds a Citadel Press edition of The Algonquin Wits.
Wikipedia gives Dorothy Parker as born Dorothy Rothschild, 22 August 1893, died 7 June 1967.
